title: Cap. VIII Arg.: God is rich in mercy — therefore he reprobates only from foresight of demerits
latin: Deus est dives in misericordia: Sed si aliquos reprobaret ex mera sua voluntate, et non propter praevisum peccatum, in tali actu nihil misericordiae appareret: Ergo reprobat ex praevisione demeritorum, sive ex praeviso malo usu liberi arbitrii ad finem usque duraturo.
pass_a: God is rich in mercy: But if he were to reprobate certain ones from his mere will, and not on account of foresighted sin, in such an act nothing of mercy would appear: Therefore he reprobates from foresight of demerits, or from the foresighted evil use of free will about to last unto the end.
pass_b: Argument: God is rich in mercy. But if he reprobated some from his mere will and not for foresighted sin, nothing of mercy would appear in that act. Therefore he reprobates from foresight of demerits — or from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end.

lemmas.gloss: rich in mercy vs mere-will reprobation
adversaries: no mercy shows without foresight sin

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Primo: we deny foresight as origin of negative reprobation, not of preparing punishment (Aquinas on Rom. 9)
latin: Primo, id semper tenendum est, Quando negamus reprobationem ex praescientia humanorum demeritorum originem habuisse, nos loqui de reprobatione quatenus significat denegatam praeparationem efficacis gratiae certis personis, non quatenus denotat praeparationem aeternae poenae iisdem personis. Nam cum Aquinate libenter concedimus: Utcunque praescientia meritorum non potest esse aliqua ratio praedestinationis, quia ipsa merita praescita cadunt sub praedestinatione, tamen praescientia peccatorum potest esse aliqua ratio reprobationis, ex parte poenae quae praeparatur reprobis, in quantum Deus proponit se puniturum malos propter peccata quae a seipsis habent, non a Deo. Haec Thomas Comment. in Rom. ix. lect. 2, prope finem.
pass_a: First, this is always to be held: When we deny that reprobation had origin from foresight of human demerits, we speak of reprobation insofar as it signifies the denied preparation of efficacious grace to certain persons, not insofar as it denotes the preparation of eternal punishment for the same persons. For with Aquinas we gladly concede: Howsoever foresight of merits cannot be any reason of predestination, because the foresighted merits themselves fall under predestination, yet foresight of sins can be some reason of reprobation, on the part of the punishment which is prepared for the reprobate, insofar as God proposes himself about to punish the evil on account of sins which they have from themselves, not from God. These things Thomas, Commentary on Romans 9, lecture 2, near the end.
pass_b: First, always hold this: when we deny that reprobation took origin from foresight of human demerits, we mean reprobation as denied preparation of efficacious grace for certain persons — not as preparation of eternal punishment for those same persons. With Aquinas we gladly grant: foresight of merits cannot be any reason of predestination, because foresighted merits themselves fall under predestination; yet foresight of sins can be some reason of reprobation on the side of the punishment prepared for the reprobate, insofar as God proposes to punish the wicked for sins they have from themselves, not from God (Thomas, Commentary on Romans 9, lect. 2, near the end).

lemmas.gloss: Aquinas: foresight sins may reason punishment side

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Secundo: reprobates regarded as bound by original guilt — rich in mercy may still elect and pass by
latin: Secundo, et illud notandum est, Eos omnes qui a Deo reprobantur, spectari ab eodem Deo ut peccati originalis reatu constrictos et damnationi obnoxios: quamvis hoc non sit simpliciter necessarium ad vindicandum Deum ab injustitia aut crudelitate, quod attinet ad reprobationem negativam, ut patet in angelis. Verum cum inter homines ita se res habeat, ut illi omnes qui reprobentur sint in se damnabiles et odio digni; Deus, quamvis dives sit in misericordia, potest aequissime pro suae voluntatis libertate ex illis quosdam eligere, quosdam reprobare, quos universos originale peccatum reddidit odio dignos et (si ita loqui liceat) reprobabiles.
pass_a: Secondly, this also is to be noted, That all those who are reprobated by God are regarded by the same God as bound by the guilt of original sin and liable to damnation: although this is not simply necessary unto vindicating God from injustice or cruelty, as to what pertains to negative reprobation, as is plain in the angels. But since among men the matter so stands, that all those who are reprobated are in themselves damnable and worthy of hatred; God, although he is rich in mercy, can most equitably according to the liberty of his will from among them elect certain ones, reprobate certain ones, whom all original sin has rendered worthy of hatred and (if it be permitted so to speak) reprobable.
pass_b: Second, note also: all whom God reprobates are regarded by him as bound by original guilt and liable to damnation — though that is not simply necessary to clear God of injustice or cruelty as to negative reprobation, as is plain in the angels. But among men it stands thus: all who are reprobated are in themselves damnable and worthy of hatred. God, though rich in mercy, can most equitably by liberty of will elect some from among them and reprobate others — all of whom original sin has made worthy of hatred and (if one may so speak) reprobable.

lemmas.gloss: rich in mercy may still freely elect and pass by

title: Cap. VIII Resp. Denique: reprobation ordered to show justice and greater mercy; some mercy even toward the reprobate
latin: Denique, quando objicitur, Si Deus reprobaret aliter quam ex praevisione finalium et actualium demeritorum, in tali actu nihil misericordiae appareret, Videtur haec objectio niti recepta quadam inter Scholasticos regula, nempe, In omnibus Dei operibus misericordiam et justitiam concurrere. Sed hujus regulae mens est, Non omnem actionem Dei esse formaliter actionem justitiae vel misericordiae, sed esse effectum Divinae providentiae ordinatum ad ostensionem vel justitiae, vel misericordiae, vel utriusque. Atque sic reprobatio haec, quam ex mera Dei voluntate factam supponimus, ordinatur ad ostensionem justitiae in damnatis, et ad ostensionem majoris misericordiae erga praedestinatos. Porro, apparet misericordia quaedam erga ipsos reprobatos, licet non illa specialis et eximia quae per gratiam efficacem infallibiliter ordinat ad gloriam. Nam reprobis conceduntur saepenumero multa gratiae ac misericordiae Divinae beneficia, quae illis non subducuntur, nisi propter abusum eorundem, et voluntariam in Deum rebellionem. Denique in ipsa damnatione horum reproborum apparet misericordia Dei, non quidem totaliter relaxans, sed aliqualiter allevians, dum punit eos citra condignum, ut bene Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 21. artic. 4.
pass_a: Finally, when it is objected, If God were to reprobate otherwise than from foresight of final and actual demerits, in such an act nothing of mercy would appear, This objection seems to rest upon a certain rule received among the Scholastics, namely, That in all the works of God mercy and justice concur. But the mind of this rule is, That not every action of God is formally an action of justice or of mercy, but is an effect of Divine providence ordained unto the showing either of justice, or of mercy, or of both. And so this reprobation, which we suppose done from the mere will of God, is ordained unto the showing of justice in the damned, and unto the showing of greater mercy toward the predestined. Further, there appears a certain mercy toward the reprobated themselves, although not that special and excellent which by efficacious grace infallibly ordains unto glory. For to the reprobate are often granted many benefits of Divine grace and mercy, which are not subtracted from them except on account of the abuse of the same, and voluntary rebellion against God. Finally in the very damnation of these reprobate there appears the mercy of God, not indeed totally relaxing, but somewhat alleviating, while he punishes them short of what is condign, as Thomas well, Part 1, question 21, article 4.
pass_b: Finally: when it is objected that if God reprobated otherwise than from foresight of final and actual demerits, nothing of mercy would appear — that objection seems to rest on a Scholastic rule: in all God's works mercy and justice concur. The sense of the rule is not that every divine action is formally an act of justice or of mercy, but that it is an effect of providence ordained to show justice, or mercy, or both. So this reprobation, which we take as from God's mere will, is ordained to show justice in the damned and greater mercy toward the predestined. Further, some mercy appears even toward the reprobate themselves — not that special excellent mercy which by efficacious grace infallibly ordains to glory, but the many benefits of grace and mercy often granted them, not withdrawn except for abuse and voluntary rebellion against God. Even in their damnation God's mercy appears — not totally relaxing, but somewhat alleviating — while he punishes them short of what is condign (Thomas, ST I, q. 21 a. 4).

lemmas.gloss: reprobation shows justice and greater mercy to elect
damnation still short of full desert (ST I q.21 a.4)

title: Cap. VIII Arg.: no just judge intends punitive justice per se — therefore God reprobates from foresight of demerit
latin: Nullus justus judex per se intendit justitiam punitivam, sed tantum ex suppositione punibilis culpae: Sed in reprobando Deus intendit justitiam suam punitivam et vindicativam exercere: Ergo reprobat ex praescientia mali et demeritorii usus liberi arbitrii.
pass_a: No just judge intends punitive justice of himself, but only upon the supposition of punishable fault: But in reprobating God intends to exercise his punitive and vindicative justice: Therefore he reprobates from foresight of the evil and demeritorious use of free will.
pass_b: They press further: a just judge never aims at punitive justice for its own sake — only once punishable fault is supposed. Yet God, they say, in the act of reprobating means to exercise punitive and vindicative justice. Hence reprobation must spring from foresight of free will's evil, demeritorious use.

lemmas.gloss: punitive justice only on supposition of fault

title: Cap. VIII Resp.: negative reprobation is not from punitive justice; permission precedes foresight of final bad use
latin: Reprobatio negativa, quae nihil aliud dicit quam aeternum Dei propositum de non-dando quibusdam singularem gratiam qua corda illorum emollirentur, cujusque beneficio ipsi ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter dirigerentur, non procedit ex justitia punitiva, neque ex voluntate damnandi, sed ex illa Divinae providentiae ratione, qua Deus judicavit sapientiae suae convenire, ut permitteret quosdam suo vitio a fine beatitudinis deficere. Posita autem hac Dei voluntate, praevidet Deus futura reproborum peccata, et finalem eorundem permansionem in peccatis; atque simul intelligit gloriae suae manifestationem ex punitione peccatorum orituram. Intendit itaque Deus justitiam punitivam exercere circa reprobates, propter peccata in quibus praevidentur vitam finitori; sed haec intentio et praevisio secuta est reprobationis praedictae actum, sicuti et ipse finalis status peccatoris in peccatis suis. Dicere quidem possumus, et vere, semper fuisse in Deo voluntatem puniendi peccata, si fierent: sed absolutam et expressam voluntatem puniendi, ac terminatam ad hanc aut illam singularem personam, non possumus in Deo ponere, nisi praesupposita Dei permissione ut fierent, utque haec persona punitioni destinata sub reatu eorundem finaliter permaneret. Haec autem permissio, quae reprobationis negativae actum continet, prior est absoluta praescientia mali usus liberi arbitrii ad finem vitae usque perdurantis in hac aut illa persona singulari, ac proinde non potest ex illa tanquam ex causa dependere. Perperam ergo reprobandi ac vindicandi sive damnandi decreta ex iisdem causis deducuntur.
pass_a: Negative reprobation, which says nothing other than the eternal purpose of God concerning not giving to certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened, and by whose benefit they themselves would be infallibly directed unto eternal life, does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from the will of damning, but from that reason of Divine providence by which God judged it to agree with his wisdom that he should permit certain ones by their own vice to fall short of the end of beatitude. But this will of God being posited, God foresights the future sins of the reprobate, and their final remaining in sins; and at the same time understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from the punishment of sins. God therefore intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobated, on account of the sins in which they are foresighted as about to finish life; but this intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as also the final state itself of the sinner in his sins. We can indeed say, and truly, that there always was in God a will of punishing sins, if they should come to be: but an absolute and express will of punishing, and terminated unto this or that singular person, we cannot place in God, unless the permission of God that they should come to be be presupposed, and that this person destined unto punishment should finally remain under the guilt of the same. But this permission, which contains the act of negative reprobation, is prior to the absolute foresight of the evil use of free will lasting unto the end of life in this or that singular person, and therefore cannot depend from that as from a cause. Wrongly therefore are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or of damning deduced from the same causes.
pass_b: Negative reprobation — nothing but God's eternal purpose not to give certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened and by which they would be infallibly directed to eternal life — does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from a will to damn, but from that reason of providence by which God judged it agreeable to his wisdom to permit some, by their own vice, to fall short of beatitude's end. That will posited, God foresights the reprobate's future sins and final remaining in them, and understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from punishing those sins. So he intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobate for the sins in which they are foresighted as finishing life — but that intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as did the sinner's final state in his sins. We may truly say there was always in God a will to punish sins if they should come to be; but an absolute express will to punish, terminated on this or that particular person, we cannot place in God unless his permission that they come to be is presupposed, and that this person destined to punishment finally remain under their guilt. That permission — which contains the act of negative reprobation — is prior to absolute foresight of evil use of free will lasting to life's end in this or that person, and so cannot depend on that foresight as cause. Wrongly, then, are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or damning drawn from the same causes.

lemmas.gloss: permission precedes foresight of final bad use
